method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)' (28 May 2018), 19 claims; LICENCE: © NT Department of Health; free copying and distribution for non-profit purposes (study, research, health service management, public information) with acknowledgement; other reproduction needs written permission (read at copyright statement on p2 of the PDF (https://digitallibrary.health.nt.gov.au/nthealthserver/api/core/bitstreams/aa3c8d5e-b046-4a13-b67e-581a9c812609/content)). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme) 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy' (2018), 10 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO (read at copyright page of the PDF (https://iris.who.int/bitstreams/bda1236a-7bde-4ff9-b6f6-86a016db8275/download)). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every edition 1.0 claim and anchor (S1, NT CDC 2018) unchanged and adds S2, the WHO 2018 leprosy guideline (GRADE), for the three-drug regimen, adult MB doses, rifampicin-resistant leprosy and single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis. S2's dose tables (Tables 3-5) extracted as clean rows in the PDF text; only the adult rows are used.

claims.claim: **Suspect leprosy when a skin lesion has definite loss of sensation (with or without thickened nerves), or a skin smear shows acid-fast bacilli:** these are the WHO cardinal signs. An Australian confirmed case needs laboratory definitive evidence (M. leprae nucleic acid) or suggestive laboratory evidence plus clinical evidence.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine the whole skin in good (ideally natural) light and in private** for macules, papules, plaques, nodules and infiltration; on darker skin patches can look copper-coloured and on lighter skin pink, and sometimes the buttocks are the only site. Test for loss of sensation, hair, pigment and sweating.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Palpate the commonly affected nerves** (ulnar, median, radial cutaneous, common peroneal, posterior tibial, sural, greater auricular, and cranial nerves 5 and 7), comparing both sides; inflamed nerves may be very tender.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine the eyes at diagnosis and every year, with annual ophthalmology slit-lamp review for silent iritis,** continuing after treatment ends. Cataract is now the commonest cause of blindness in leprosy.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **WHO: diagnose on clinical examination, adding a slit-skin smear or biopsy histology where available.** Newer ELISA, lateral-flow and PCR tests offer no clear gain over this, and no test is advised to detect latent infection in well contacts (only 4% of test-positive contacts went on to develop leprosy).
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Baseline tests before MDT:** FBE, electrolytes/renal function, LFTs, hepatitis B and C and HIV serology, G6PD, Mantoux and chest X-ray (to exclude TB or latent TB), and an ECG for prolonged QTc.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **MDT is the worldwide standard: it cures the individual, limits resistance and interrupts transmission.** If the classification is uncertain or the skin smear is positive, treat as multibacillary.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Paucibacillary leprosy, age 15 and over: self-administered dapsone 100 mg daily plus rifampicin 600 mg once a month for 6 months.** Single-lesion disease is treated the same way.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Multibacillary leprosy: 12 months if the bacillary index is below 4+, but at least 24 months if it is 4+ or more.** This is longer than the WHO's 12 months for all MB disease, because a high bacillary index carries more relapse; the US National Hansen's Disease Program also advises 24 months.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monthly doses are directly observed** (4-weekly dosing on the same weekday is easier in practice). Dispense weekly at first until adherence is secure; a single missed 4-weekly visit needs immediate tracing.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Completion means all doses within a window:** 24 monthly cycles within 36 months (MB, BI 4+ or more), 12 within 18 months (MB, BI below 4+) or 6 within 9 months (PB). Anyone who does not complete needs full re-evaluation.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **WHO gives every patient the same three drugs, rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine: 6 months for PB and 12 months for MB.** Adult doses: rifampicin 600 mg once a month, clofazimine 300 mg once a month plus 50 mg daily, and dapsone 100 mg daily. This differs from S1, which gives PB disease two drugs and a longer MB course when the bacillary index is high.
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Why three drugs for PB:** about 10–14 more patients per 100 had a good outcome at 12 months, and 26 more per 100 at 24 months, and a third drug protects MB patients wrongly counted as PB. Where a PB patient is very worried about clofazimine skin darkening, the two-drug regimen can be considered.
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **WHO does not shorten MB treatment to 6 months:** in the one randomised trial, relapse was 2.2% after 6 months against 0.3% after 12 (not statistically significant, but a signal).
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Children 10–14 years get the WHO fixed child doses with specialist input; under 10 years, or under 40 kg, doses are reduced proportionately and should be discussed with a TB/ID physician or paediatrician.**
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pregnancy: continue standard MDT,** because leprosy worsens in pregnancy; the drugs pass into breast milk, but the only reported infant effect is mild temporary skin discolouration from clofazimine.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Leprosy with active TB needs full treatment of both;** rifampicin is shared and should be given at the TB dose. With latent TB, a rifampicin-containing MDT given daily for at least 4 months also treats the LTBI. HIV co-infection needs no change to either regimen.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use alternative regimens only for severe side effects or contraindications, and only with a specialist leprosy service.**
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Rifampicin resistance is uncommon but real:** about 1.4% of new and 8% of relapsed patients in the studies WHO reviewed. A patient found resistant after starting MDT restarts a full second-line course whatever the clinical response.
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Rifampicin-resistant leprosy: for 6 months give clofazimine 50 mg daily with at least two of ofloxacin 400 mg, minocycline 100 mg or clarithromycin 500 mg daily; then clofazimine with one of them for 18 more months.** If ofloxacin resistance is also present, leave out quinolones and use clarithromycin, minocycline and clofazimine. Levofloxacin 500 mg or moxifloxacin 400 mg can stand in for ofloxacin. This rests on expert opinion.
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Before a second-line regimen, look for TB,** because quinolones treat TB and a missed case risks drug-resistant TB. Monitor the ECG: clarithromycin, minocycline and quinolones can prolong the QT interval.
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Give prednisolone for:** nerve function impairment under 12 months old at diagnosis; new impairment during or after MDT; any type 1 reaction (start with MDT if present at diagnosis); moderate or severe ENL (type 2) or ENL with neuritis; or worsening nerve conduction.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Prednisolone typically starts at 1 mg/kg (60 mg in adults) for a severe reaction with neuritis, or 40 mg for silent neuropathy or a mild reaction,** then tapers by about 5 mg every 1–2 weeks once controlled; severe reactions usually need 3–6 months. Keep MDT going throughout.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recurrent reactions: high-dose clofazimine, 300 mg daily for 3 months, then 100 mg daily until reactions stop.** Screen for opportunistic infections before any prednisolone.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine household, family and close social contacts;** shared-bedroom contacts and children in the household are at highest risk. Review contacts of multibacillary cases every year for 5 years; contacts of paucibacillary cases need one examination.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Offer all household contacts a single dose of rifampicin as chemoprophylaxis unless contraindicated** (600 mg over 35 kg, 450 mg at 20–35 kg, 10–15 mg/kg under 20 kg). In a trial it cut contacts' risk by 57% over two years.
claims.locator: Centre for Disease Control, Department of Health, Northern Territory Government, 'Guidelines for the control of leprosy in the Northern Territory, Version 3.0 (fourth edition)', 28 May 2018, https://hdl.handle.net/10137/526, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **WHO: single-dose rifampicin for contacts aged 2 years and over,** once leprosy and TB have been excluded and there is no other contraindication, and only where contacts can be managed and the index patient agrees to disclosure. WHO doses by age: 600 mg from 15 years, 450 mg at 10–14 years, 300 mg at 6–9 years (20 kg or more), 10–15 mg/kg under 20 kg.
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Expected benefit:** in the COLEP trial, risk fell by 57% over 2 years and 30% over 5–6 years (about four cases prevented per 1000 contacts treated at 1–2 years); BCG at birth appeared to raise protection to 80%.
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Respect the patient's choice about disclosure:** if they do not agree, WHO advises against tracing or screening their contacts, which rules out prophylaxis for them.
claims.locator: World Health Organization, Regional Office for South-East Asia (Global Leprosy Programme), 'Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of leprosy', 2018, https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/274127, retrieved 2026-09-24
